lines.text: Terrance Watanabe ran his family's party-supply company in Omaha for over twenty years.
Then he sold it, and found Las Vegas.
His drinking got so bad that one casino, the Wynn, banned him.
Caesars Palace and the Rio did the opposite.
They gave him a bellman of his own, and a personal security guard.
On big losses, he reportedly got fifteen percent back.
In two thousand seven, by his own count, he bet more than eight hundred and twenty-five million dollars.
He lost nearly a hundred and twenty-seven million.
That one man was five point six percent of the company's Las Vegas gambling revenue.
Three casino workers later said he was drunk almost every time he played.

lines.text: Some nights he fell asleep at the table, woke up, and kept betting.
His sister finally stepped in, and he went to rehab.
He had paid back almost everything.
But fourteen point seven million dollars stayed unpaid.
So the casino took him to the district attorney.
He was charged with four felonies, and faced up to twenty-eight years.
His answer: the casino had kept him drunk to keep him playing.
In the end, the charges were dropped, and both sides settled in private.
Years later, New Jersey regulators fined Caesars two hundred and twenty-five thousand dollars over how it handled him.
That's less than a fifth of one percent of what he lost.
So when a casino's best customer can't stand up, who is supposed to say stop?
